spans.text: Due to differences in colonial history and language influences in the two islands, Trinidad English Creole differs markedly from Tobago English Creole; only the former will be considered here.
Trinidad English Creole is spoken by some 1,200,000 people in the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, an archipelagic state consisting of two main islands, Trinidad and Tobago.
There is substantial phonological variation between lower and upper mesolectal forms of Trinidad English Creole vowel use.
Two principal Amerindian linguistic-cultural groups, the Arawaks and the Caribs, inhabited Trinidad at the time of the first European contact in 1498, when Columbus gave the island its modern name.
Today, Trinidad French Creole is almost extinct.

In order to substitute labour on the plantations, immigrants were recruited at first from the British colonies St Helena (3,198) and from former slave ships via Sierra Leone (3,383; Brereton 1981: 98).

After the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807, the inter-island slave trade, although illegal, still prospered in the Caribbean.
